analysis.one_liner: Requires Medicare to negotiate the lowest possible prescription drug prices and disclose them publicly.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee without a hearing, a vote, or a single cosponsor, and the ban on Medicare drug-price negotiation stayed in effect.
analysis.plain_summary: The 2003 Medicare drug benefit law contained a 'non-interference' clause that barred the Secretary of Health and Human Services from negotiating drug prices with manufacturers. This bill would have struck that clause and required the Secretary to negotiate the lowest possible prices for Medicare beneficiaries, with the same bulk-buying authority used by the Department of Veterans Affairs and the military, and to publish the negotiated prices. It was referred to two committees and their Health subcommittees and never received a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare beneficiaries, tens of millions of seniors and disabled Americans, would have gained if the government used its buying power to push down the prices they and their drug plans pay. Taxpayers would also have benefited, since public money helps cover Medicare drug costs.

how_it_helps.text: The bill struck the 'non-interference' clause and replaced it with a requirement that the Secretary of Health and Human Services negotiate the best possible prices for drugs covered by the Medicare drug benefit.
It modeled the Secretary's authority on agencies that buy drugs in bulk, such as the Department of Veterans Affairs, which historically pays some of the lowest drug prices in the country.
It required the Secretary to widely disseminate the negotiated prices, so beneficiaries and the public could see what Medicare was paying.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name drug manufacturers would bear the cost, since Medicare negotiation modeled on the VA's bulk buying would cut into their prices and revenue on one of the largest drug markets in the world.

drawbacks.text: Critics of giving the Secretary negotiation authority argue it amounts to government price-setting, which could reduce drug makers' revenue and, over time, their incentives to develop new medicines.

The bill is one page long and offers no mechanism for how the Secretary's negotiated prices would work alongside the private Part D plans created by the 2003 Medicare law — a design gap that could have created conflict between government-negotiated prices and plan formularies.
The bill received no committee hearing, no cost estimate, and no vote, so its real-world costs and savings were never analyzed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The potential benefit was large: millions of seniors and disabled beneficiaries pay out of pocket for medicines, and the government itself was the biggest buyer, so using that leverage could have lowered prices significantly, as it does for veterans and the military. The costs are real but unmeasured — the bill was one page long and left the hard questions unanswered: how the Secretary's negotiation would mesh with private plans, whether it would narrow the drugs available, and what it would do to manufacturers' research incentives. It received no hearing, no committee vote, and no independent cost estimate, so there was no record on which to weigh the tradeoffs.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees, then to their Health subcommittees, and no committee ever took it up before the 108th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Stephen Lynch introduced H.R. 4321 on May 10, 2004.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and the Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced.
In mid-May 2004 both committees referred it to their Health subcommittees, which took no further action.
No other House member signed on as a cosponsor, and the bill never received a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 108th Congress ended on January 3, 2005.

The bill targeted the 'non-interference' provision of the 2003 Medicare drug law, which barred the Secretary of Health and Human Services from interfering in price negotiations between drug makers and plans.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name drug manufacturers came out ahead: the non-interference clause stayed in place and the government remained barred from negotiating drug prices for Medicare beneficiaries.

for.name: Rep. Stephen F. Lynch
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill; it attracted no cosponsors.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and referred it to the Health Subcommittee; never held a hearing or markup.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and referred it to the Health Subcommittee; never took further action.

against.name: Pharmaceutical research and manufacturing industry
against.what_they_did: Fought efforts to let the government negotiate Medicare drug prices and defended the non-interference clause this bill would have repealed.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no other member cosponsored, so the record shows only a lone Democratic sponsor and no way to gauge how the parties would have split.

industries.note: The bill repealed the 'non-interference' clause that kept the government from negotiating, and required the Secretary to negotiate the best possible prices for Medicare-covered drugs, modeled on the bulk-buying power of the VA. Lower prices would come directly out of manufacturer revenue on the biggest drug-purchasing program in the country.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and private drug plans
industries.note: The non-interference clause barred the Secretary from interfering with negotiations between drug makers and plans or PBMs. Government negotiation could have squeezed the intermediaries' role and margins in Part D, though private plans would have remained the delivery channel.
